![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14227209/assets/ebe962cc3394e0839d77fba922a5a7f56f31201f6926ef8b4236c1f82edd2e90.png)

Consider a right triangle inscribed in a semicircle of radius
$5,$ as shown above. What is the greatest possible perimeter of the triangle?
questions.worked_solution:
Let's call $l$ the length of one of the legs. By the Pythagorean theorem, the length of the other leg is $\sqrt{100-{l}^{2}}.$

Therefore, the perimeter is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}P(l) & =10+l+\sqrt{100-{l}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $l$ is the length of a leg of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is $10,$ the permitted range of $l$ is $0<l<10.$

We want to maximize $P(l),$ so we need to compute the critical points. Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(l) & =1+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{-2l}{\sqrt{100-{l}^{2}}} \\  & =1-\frac{l}{\sqrt{100-{l}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${P}^{′}(l)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(l) & =0 \\ 1-\frac{l}{\sqrt{100-{l}^{2}}} & =0 \\ \frac{l}{\sqrt{100-{l}^{2}}} & =1 \\ l & =\sqrt{100-{l}^{2}} \\ {l}^{2} & =100-{l}^{2} \\ 2{l}^{2} & =100 \\ {l}^{2} & =50 \\ l & =5\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

All that's left now is to confirm that $l=5\sqrt{2}$ does indeed give a maximum value of $P(l).$ To do this, we use the first derivative test. We write up a table of values:

| Interval | $(0,5\sqrt{2})$ | $5\sqrt{2}$ | $(5\sqrt{2},10)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ | $$ | $8$ |
| ${P}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $P$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

So $l=5\sqrt{2}$ does indeed give a maximum, and the perimeter of the resulting triangle will be the largest possible.

Therefore, the greatest perimeter that a triangle can have is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(5\sqrt{2}) & =10+5\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{100-(5\sqrt{2})^{2}} \\  & =10+5\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{100-50} \\  & =10+5\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{50} \\  & =10+5\sqrt{2}+5\sqrt{2} \\  & =10+10\sqrt{2} \\  & =10(1+\sqrt{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider a right triangle inscribed in a semicircle of radius
$5\sqrt{2}.$ If the hypotenuse of the triangle lies along the diameter of the semicircle, what is the greatest possible perimeter of the triangle?
questions.worked_solution:
We first draw a picture of the situation:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14227209/assets/296e866a3104f0d2a7891726274578bcdffb84853ce896e8723e2b742d22ac27.png)

Let's call $l$ the length of one of the legs. By the Pythagorean theorem, the length of the other leg is $\sqrt{200-{l}^{2}}.$

Therefore, the perimeter is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}P(l) & =10\sqrt{2}+l+\sqrt{200-{l}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $l$ is the length of a leg of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is $10\sqrt{2},$ the permitted range of $l$ is $0<l<10\sqrt{2}.$

We want to maximize $P(l),$ so we need to compute the critical points. Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(l) & =1+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{-2l}{\sqrt{200-{l}^{2}}} \\  & =1-\frac{l}{\sqrt{200-{l}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${P}^{′}(l)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(l) & =0 \\ 1-\frac{l}{\sqrt{200-{l}^{2}}} & =0 \\ \frac{l}{\sqrt{200-{l}^{2}}} & =1 \\ l & =\sqrt{200-{l}^{2}} \\ {l}^{2} & =200-{l}^{2} \\ 2{l}^{2} & =200 \\ {l}^{2} & =100 \\ l & =10\end{aligned}
$$

All that's left now is to confirm that $l=10$ does indeed give a maximum value of $P(l).$ To do this, we use the first derivative test. We write up a table of values:

| Interval | $(0,10)$ | $10$ | $(10,10\sqrt{2})$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ | $$ | $11$ |
| ${P}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $P$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

So, $l=10$ does indeed give a maximum, and the perimeter of the resulting triangle will be the largest possible.

Therefore, the greatest perimeter that a triangle can have is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(10) & =10\sqrt{2}+10+\sqrt{200-{10}^{2}} \\  & =10\sqrt{2}+10+\sqrt{200-100} \\  & =10\sqrt{2}+10+\sqrt{100} \\  & =10\sqrt{2}+10+10 \\  & =10\sqrt{2}+20 \\  & =10(2+\sqrt{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider a right triangle inscribed in a semicircle of radius $10\sqrt{2}.$ If the hypotenuse of the triangle lies along the diameter of the semicircle, find the maximum possible area of the triangle.
questions.worked_solution:
We first draw a picture of the situation:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14227209/assets/172826a7fa27ac8957f120e15622cf0c96b0e8df66e5f6fd3d7d99ab0b32c5f0.png)

Let's call $l$ the length of one leg. By the Pythagorean theorem, the length of the other leg is $\sqrt{800-{l}^{2}}.$

Therefore, the area of the triangle is given by

$$
A(l)=\frac{1}{2}l\sqrt{800-{l}^{2}}\,.
$$

Since $l$ is the length of a leg of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is $20\sqrt{2}$, the permitted range of $l$ is $0<l<20\sqrt{2}.$

We want to maximize $A(l),$ so we need to compute the critical points. Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(l) & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{800-{l}^{2}}-\frac{{l}^{2}}{2\sqrt{800-{l}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${A}^{′}(l)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(l) & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{800-{l}^{2}}-\frac{{l}^{2}}{2\sqrt{800-{l}^{2}}} & =0 \\ 800-{l}^{2}-{l}^{2} & =0 \\ {l}^{2} & =\frac{800}{2} \\ {l}^{2} & =400 \\ l & =20\end{aligned}
$$

All that's left now is to confirm that $l=20$ does indeed give a maximum value of $A(l).$ To do this, we use the first derivative test. We write up a table of values:

| Interval | $(0,20)$ | $20$ | $(20,20\sqrt{2})$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ | $$ | $25$ |
| ${A}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $A$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

So, $l=20$ does indeed give a maximum, and the area of the resulting triangle will be the largest possible.

Finally, the maximum possible area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A(20) & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 20\cdot \sqrt{800-{(20)}^{2}} \\  & =10\cdot \sqrt{800-400} \\  & =10\cdot \sqrt{400} \\  & =10\cdot 20 \\  & =200.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Let's call $l$ the length of one leg. By the Pythagorean theorem, the length of the other leg is $\sqrt{256-{l}^{2}}.$

Therefore, the area of the triangle is given by

$$
A(l)=\frac{1}{2}l\sqrt{256-{l}^{2}}\,.
$$

Since $l$ is the length of a leg of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is $16$, the permitted range of $l$ is $0<l<16.$

We want to maximize $A(l),$ so we need to compute the critical points. Taking the derivative, we get

$$
{A}^{′}(l)=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{256-{l}^{2}}-\frac{{l}^{2}}{2\sqrt{256-{l}^{2}}}.
$$

and solving ${A}^{′}(l)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{256-{l}^{2}}-\frac{{l}^{2}}{2\sqrt{256-{l}^{2}}} & =0 \\ 256-{l}^{2}-{l}^{2} & =0 \\ 2{l}^{2} & =256 \\ {l}^{2} & =128 \\ l & =8\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

All that's left now is to confirm that $l=8\sqrt{2}$ does indeed give a maximum value of $A(l).$ To do this, we use the first derivative test. We write up a table of values:

| Interval | $(0,8\sqrt{2})$ | $8\sqrt{2}$ | $(8\sqrt{2},16)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ | $$ | $12$ |
| ${A}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $A$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

So, $l=8\sqrt{2}$ does indeed give a maximum, and the area of the resulting triangle will be the largest possible.

Finally, the maximum possible area ${A}_{\text{max}}$  is

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{\text{max}}=A(8\sqrt{2}) & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 8\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{256-(8\sqrt{2})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 8\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{128} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 8\sqrt{2}\cdot 8\sqrt{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 64\cdot 2 \\  & =64.\end{aligned}
$$
